blocks.text: Bondi’s café scene is as iconic as its golden stretch of sand, buzzing from sunrise swims to late brunch catch-ups. Whether you’re chasing a post-surf flat white or a long, lazy breakfast, these standout spots capture the best of Bondi right now.

Start at Lamrock Cafe, where sweeping ocean views and a relaxed, family-run atmosphere make it a go-to for both locals and visitors. Just a short stroll away, Harry’s delivers the quintessential Bondi vibe, light-filled, beachy, and known for creative, seasonal dishes that celebrate fresh local produce.

For something quick but consistently excellent, Pocket and The Depot are neighbourhood favourites, perfect for takeaway coffee or a casual brunch. If you’re after something a little more elevated, Blackwood stands out with its Mediterranean-inspired menu and inventive drinks, making it one of Bondi’s most talked-about brunch spots.

Health-conscious? Up South and Chapter One offer fresh, nourishing options that reflect Bondi’s wellness culture, think vibrant bowls, smoothies, and quality coffee. Meanwhile, Glory Days brings a fun, energetic feel to the café scene, and Shuk blends Middle Eastern flavours with classic café staples, serving up everything from Israeli breakfasts to pastries in a lively setting.

Bondi’s cafés are more than just places to eat, they’re where the community comes together. From beachfront icons to tucked-away gems, these spots showcase why Bondi remains one of Australia’s ultimate café destinations.

blocks.text: Bondi Beach is one of Australia’s most iconic coastal destinations - renowned for its golden sands, crystal-clear waters, vibrant surf culture, world-class cafés, and laid-back Aussie lifestyle. Whether you’re a first-time visitor or returning traveller, this guide will help you plan the perfect trip - from how to get here and when to visit, to the best things to do and local insider tips.
What Makes Bondi Beach Special

Located just 7 km east of Sydney’s CBD, Bondi Beach stretches about 1 km and attracts visitors from all over the world. It’s more than just a beach - it’s a cultural hotspot where surf meets lifestyle. Bondi blends natural beauty with outdoor experiences, seaside dining, boutique shopping, and immersive beach culture that keeps visitors coming back year after year.
How to Get to Bondi Beach
From Sydney Airport
Taxi or Uber takes around 20–30 minutes depending on traffic.
Train and bus combination: Take a train to Town Hall or Central Station, then catch a direct bus to Bondi Beach.
From Sydney CBD
Bus services run frequently from Circular Quay, Town Hall, and Martin Place.
Driving is possible, but parking fills up quickly during peak summer months, so arrive early.
Best Time to Visit
Bondi Beach is great year-round, but the prime time to visit is during spring (September to November) and autumn (March to May). These seasons offer mild weather, warm water, and fewer crowds.
Summer (December to February) is peak season, delivering the liveliest atmosphere, busy beaches, and strong surf conditions.
Top Things to Do in Bondi Beach
Swim and Sunbathe

Bondi’s crescent of sand is ideal for relaxing. Always swim between the red and yellow flags where lifeguards patrol. The southern end of the beach is known for strong currents, so inexperienced swimmers should take extra care.
Bondi to Coogee Coastal Walk

This scenic cliffside walk is one of Sydney’s most famous experiences. The full 6 km route takes approximately two to three hours and offers stunning ocean views, parks, rock pools, and smaller beaches along the way.
Bondi Icebergs and Ocean Pools
The Bondi Icebergs Club features a famous ocean pool overlooking the surf. It is open year-round and offers one of the most photographed swimming experiences in Australia.
Surfing and Water Sports
Bondi’s waves are legendary. Surf schools and board rentals operate daily, making it easy for beginners to learn and experienced surfers to enjoy the break.
Dining and Cafés
Bondi’s food scene is a major attraction. Expect beachfront brunch spots, fresh seafood restaurants, health-focused cafés, and vibrant coffee culture.
Art and Culture
Bondi is home to the Bondi Pavilion, street art along the sea wall, and annual events such as Sculpture by the Sea and Festival of the Winds.
Where to Stay
Accommodation ranges from luxury hotels with ocean views to boutique guesthouses and budget hostels. Booking well in advance is recommended during summer and holiday periods.
Travel Tips and Local Insights
Arrive early during summer to secure parking and enjoy cooler morning conditions.
Public transport using an Opal card is often more convenient than driving.
Always follow lifeguard instructions and local beach safety guidelines.

Bondi Beach is more than just a place to visit - it’s a defining Sydney experience. From sunrise swims and scenic coastal walks to relaxed long lunches and world-famous surf, Bondi captures the essence of Australia’s coastal lifestyle. Plan your trip well, take your time exploring, and you’ll quickly understand why Bondi remains one of the most visited beaches in the world.

title: The Bondi Lifeguards Who Ran Toward Danger
metaDescription: The inside story of the Bondi lifeguards and surf lifesavers who ran toward danger - courage, training and instinct on Sydney's most famous beach.
h1: The Inside Story On The Bondi Lifeguards Who Ran Toward Danger
intro: The Inside Story On The Bondi Lifeguards Who Ran Toward Danger — Visit Bondi Beach Visit Bondi Beach Bondi Beach Guide What's On Swim Accommodation Tours Bondi Icebergs Gallery About Bondi Beach Guide What's On Swim Accommodation Tours Bondi Icebergs Gallery About Visit Bondi Beach The Inside Story On The Bondi Lifeguards Who Ran Toward Danger When terror struck Bondi, instinct, courage and training took over. As panic rippled across the beachfront, Bondi’s lifeguards and surf lifesaving v

blocks.text: When terror struck Bondi, instinct, courage and training took over. As panic rippled across the beachfront, Bondi’s lifeguards and surf lifesaving volunteers did not hesitate. They ran toward the sound of gunfire, placing themselves between danger and the public.

Daniel McLaughlin, known to his colleagues as “Beardy,” was among the first to respond. Hearing gunshots, he immediately led a team of lifeguards toward the scene to assist and assess the unfolding emergency. At the same time, Jackson Doolan - “Jacko” - sprinted barefoot from Tamarama to Bondi, carrying a defibrillator across the sand, determined to help however he could.

Out on the water, junior lifeguard Rory Davey noticed two swimmers struggling amid the chaos. As gunfire echoed, he paddled out and brought them safely to shore. While Rory was in the water, Lukas Street - known as “Boo” - positioned his lifeguard buggy to shield beachgoers from harm, using it as a barrier between civilians and the threat.

Other lifeguards were already on patrol when the attack began. Michael Jenkinson and Mario Marfella were among the first on the scene, assisting victims and coordinating with emergency services. Lifeguards Michael Jenkinson (“Mouse”), Trent Maxwell (“Maxi”) and Trent Falson (“Singlets”) were also seen providing hands-on support, helping first responders treat the injured.
Alongside them, volunteers from the Bondi and North Bondi Surf Life Saving Clubs stepped up as first responders, offering critical aid in the moments before police and paramedics arrived.
In one of Australia’s darkest moments, the bravery of these lifeguards and volunteers stood as a powerful reminder of community, selflessness and quiet heroism.
Right now, the local surf clubs are raising money to replace supplies used during the attack. You can donate here: https://slsfoundation.com.au/campaign/bondi

blocks.text: Sydney’s coastline is once again set to transform into an open-air gallery as Sculpture by the Sea returns for its annual run from Bondi to Tamarama. Mark your calendars - this year’s edition promises over 100 captivating sculptures from both Australian and international artists, and entry is completely free.
Where & When
Route: The coastal walk between Bondi Beach and Tamarama Beach
Dates: Opens October 18 and runs through November 4
Hours: Daily, from sunrise to sunset
Cost: Free admission
A Cultural Start to Sydney’s Summer

Sculpture by the Sea has long been heralded as one of the defining cultural events that ushers in summer in Sydney. Over its 18-day duration, it’s expected to attract around 450,000 visitors who come to experience art in a breathtaking natural setting.

This year’s installations will run the gamut from whimsical and humorous (think melting ice-cream trucks or oversized lobsters) to abstract and gravity-defying constructs. The contrast between the sculptures and the dramatic seascape is part of what makes this event so magical.
A Legacy of Growth

What began as a one-day, volunteer-run show with just 64 local artists and a modest crowd of 25,000 has evolved into the world’s largest free outdoor sculpture exhibition. Over time, Sculpture by the Sea has inspired spin-offs elsewhere in Australia - Perth, for example, now hosts its own Cottesloe edition that’s become a fixture in its cultural calendar.
Highlights to Keep an Eye On
Even though the full line-up is revealed closer to the launch, past editions hint at what you might see (we also don’t want to ruin the surprise!)
Playful, large-scale installations that invite closer inspection
Sculptures that contrast with or echo the surrounding ocean and cliffs
Works from international as well as Australian artists
Bold and provocative pieces that spark conversation
Tips for Visiting
Go early or late in the day to avoid crowds and catch softer light for photography
Wear comfortable shoes - the promenade is about 2 km
Bring sun protection, water, and a camera
Take your time: sculptures appear and disappear depending on the tide and shifting light
Check the official site (sculpturebythesea.com) closer to opening for the full artist directory and map

blocks.text: Only one, and his name is Blake.

If you’ve wandered down Blair Street lately, you might have spotted a curious creature slithering its way along the footpath. Don’t panic-this isn’t the sort of snake that’ll send you running for your life. It’s the friendliest serpent in Sydney: Blake the Blair Street Snake, a growing community art project made entirely of painted rocks.
It all starts with a single boulder-Blake’s cheerful head-painted a minty green with pink and black patches, perched proudly beside a sign that reads:
“I’m Blake the Blair St Snake. Add a painted rock to see how long I can get :)”

From there, a colourful line of rocks-each one unique, each one clearly made with love-winds its way down the stone wall like scales on a giant, happy reptile. Some are splashed in pastels, others are flecked with stars or faces, and a few look like they were painted by very small (and very enthusiastic) hands. The result is a delightful collision of creativity and community spirit, stretching further every week as locals and passers-by contribute to Blake’s ever-lengthening body.

It’s hard not to smile when you stumble across him. In a world of “Do Not Touch” signs and digital distractions, here’s a simple invitation to join in. No permissions, no forms-just grab a rock, grab some paint, and make your mark. Kids love it. Parents love it. Even joggers pause mid-stride to admire the growing serpent before continuing their run toward the beach.

There’s something quietly magical about the whole thing. Each rock tells a tiny story: maybe painted during lockdown, maybe created during a weekend craft session, maybe left behind by a visitor wanting to be part of something local. Blake is like Bondi’s community diary-only instead of words, it’s written in colour.

And while Bondi might be famous for its shimmering water, perfect surf, and occasional shark sighting, this particular reptile has become something just as iconic in its own quirky way. He represents that easygoing, creative energy that makes Bondi what it is-where art doesn’t always live in galleries, and community can grow one painted stone at a time.

So next time you’re wandering Blair Street, keep an eye out. Bring a rock, add your touch, and help Blake slither a little further. Whether you’re a local legend or just passing through, he’s always happy to have new friends join the chain.
Because yes, there is a snake in Bondi.
Just one.
And he’s the kind that makes everyone smile.

blocks.text: Event Overview & Dates
Date: Sunday, 31 August 2025 - the official Abbott World Marathon Major debut for Sydney, drawing around 35,000 marathon runners .
Race Distances: Full Marathon (42.195 km), 10 km Bridge Run, and a 4.2 km Mini Marathon-ideal for family or casual participation .
Logistics & Travel
Start and Finish Locations
Start Line: At North Sydney Oval (Bradfield Park / Milsons Point) .
Finish Line: Forecourt of the Sydney Opera House .
Public Transport Access
Free public transport is included with entry-highly encouraged over driving .
Start Group Access:
Groups A, B, E, F → Victoria Cross or North Sydney Station
Groups C, D → Crows Nest Station
Road Closures & Clearways
Significant road closures between 2 am and 4 pm across areas including the Harbour Bridge, CBD, and Moore Park. Driving is strongly discouraged .
Be aware of special-event clearway restrictions-vehicles may be towed if improperly parked .
Marathon Expo (“Running Show”)
Held 28–30 August at the ICC Sydney (Darling Drive) .
Bib pickup requires your assigned QR code and matching ID. Friends/family cannot collect your bib for you .
Course Overview & Terrain
Course Highlights
Begin over the Sydney Harbour Bridge, then flow through The Rocks, Circular Quay, Hyde Park, Moore Park, Centennial Parklands, and the Eastern Suburbs, finally returning to the Opera House .
Elevation & Strategy
Expect ~317 meters of elevation gain-one of the hillier courses among the World Marathon Majors.
The course includes rolling hills; most elevation gain is spread out, with a notable downhill toward the finish.
Training & Pre-Race Tips
16-Week Training Structure
Weeks 1–6 (Base Building): 3–4 runs/week, gradually increasing long runs to ~24–28 km; include strides and cross-training .
Weeks 7–12 (Strength & Speed): Incorporate hill workouts and tempo sessions (implied, follow logical next phase) .
Specific Preparations
Hill Workouts: Essential for building strength. Include both uphill runs and downhill strength training (e.g., lunges) .
Familiarization: If possible, train on parts of the course-including the Harbour Bridge and Centennial Parklands .
Race Day Essentials & Logistics
Start Line & Wave Management
Start waves begin from 6:30 am, following an elite wheelchair wave at 6:15 am .
Bag drop is only available at the expo; bring only the provided bag. On race morning, unregistered bags will be discarded .
Arrive early and plan where you’ll enter your wave. Rest by sitting on disposable material to save energy .
Strict cut-off: No runners allowed to cross start line after 8:15 am .
Gear, Weather & Warmth
Early mornings can be cold-bring throwaway layers, gloves, or blankets for warmth (and discard at start) .
Weather conditions may range from cool to potential warmth-plan clothing and hydration accordingly .
Recovery & Post-Race
Immediate Steps
Hydrate and refuel with a mix of protein and carbohydrates shortly after finishing .
Light stretching or walking in the nearby Royal Botanic Gardens or Centennial Parklands can aid recovery .
Additional Advice
Pack smart for race day: essentials include bib and safety pins, GPS watch, weather-appropriate gear, fuel, anti-chafe supplies, post-race clothing and snacks .
Beginner mistakes to avoid: taper properly in the last week; don’t introduce new foods or gear on race day; know the course layout; arrive early and plan logistics; and avoid starting too fast .

blocks.text: In the days leading up to the Sydney Marathon, training takes a back seat to one of the most important parts of race preparation: fuelling. Carb loading is a tried-and-tested method for marathon runners, helping to maximise glycogen stores in your muscles so you have the energy to power through 42.2 kilometres.

Whether you’re a local runner or flying in from overseas, Sydney offers fantastic dining options for pre-race meals - from hearty bowls of pasta to fresh bakery breads. Bondi Beach, just a short trip from the city centre, is a standout spot for runners looking to combine quality carbs with a world-class coastal atmosphere.
This guide covers the best carb-loading restaurants in Bondi and Sydney, plus tips on how to eat smart in the final days before race day.
Why Carb Loading Matters

Carbohydrates are stored in your muscles as glycogen, your body’s primary energy source during endurance events. When glycogen stores run low, fatigue sets in - the dreaded “hitting the wall.” By increasing your carb intake in the 2–3 days before the race, you can top up these stores and give yourself the best chance of maintaining pace through the finish line.

Pro Tip: Carb loading is not about eating as much pasta as possible in one sitting. Spread your intake over several meals, choose familiar foods your stomach tolerates well, and avoid excess fibre or rich, fatty sauces.
Top Carb-Loading Spots in Bondi
Bondi Trattoria

A local institution, Bondi Trattoria is a favourite among visiting runners for its combination of hearty Italian dishes and relaxed, beachside location. The seafood linguine is a lighter option that still packs plenty of carbs, while the pumpkin ravioli delivers a comforting, satisfying pre-race meal. Their outdoor tables overlook the southern end of Bondi Beach - perfect for soaking up the atmosphere without straying too far from your accommodation.
Pompei’s

If fresh pasta is non-negotiable for your carb load, Pompei’s is the place to go. Their house-made pasta is rolled daily, and pizzas come with thin, crisp bases that won’t leave you feeling heavy. For marathon prep, the spaghetti pomodoro is simple, effective, and easy to digest. The restaurant has a lively, community feel, making it a great spot to meet up with fellow runners.
Lox Stock & Barrel

Not every carb-loading meal has to be Italian. Lox Stock & Barrel, a New York-style deli and café, serves bagels, sourdough sandwiches, and grain bowls that are ideal for breakfast or lunch carb boosts. Try a plain bagel with smoked salmon for a balanced, runner-friendly meal, or their wholegrain salad with an extra bread roll for sustained energy.
Sonoma Bakery

For portable carb sources, head to Sonoma Bakery and stock up on sourdough, fruit loaf, and banana bread. These are perfect for snacks or light meals the day before the race. Having easy, familiar foods on hand is especially helpful if you’re staying in self-catered accommodation or need a quick bite between marathon events.
Carb-Loading Gems in the Sydney CBD
If you’re staying near the start line or want to combine a city visit with your carb load, the CBD has excellent runner-friendly options.
Fratelli Fresh

With multiple locations in Sydney, including a large venue in Darling Harbour, Fratelli Fresh is a reliable choice for pre-race pasta. Their pappardelle bolognese and penne arrabbiata are generous but not overly rich. Portions are big enough to share if you’re loading gradually.
Macchiato Wood Fire Pizza & Coffee Roastery
Located near Town Hall, Macchiato offers wood-fired pizzas with thin crusts and quality toppings. Their margherita is a safe, carb-heavy choice that won’t upset your stomach.
Pasta Emilia
For organic, hand-made pasta in a cosy setting, Pasta Emilia in Surry Hills is a standout. The tagliatelle with slow-cooked tomato sauce is ideal for runners looking for simple, clean flavours.
How to Eat Smart Before the Sydney Marathon
1. Start 2–3 Days Out
Gradually increase your carbohydrate percentage to about 70% of total calories. Keep protein and healthy fats in your diet, but make carbs the main focus.
2. Keep It Familiar
Now is not the time to experiment with spicy sauces, exotic grains, or high-fibre breads you’ve never eaten before. Stick to foods you know your body digests well.
3. Don’t Forget Hydration
Carbs are stored with water, so increase your fluid intake. Avoid excess alcohol and limit caffeine to your usual amounts.
4. Spread Your Intake
Rather than a single giant pasta dinner, aim for moderate carb portions at each meal. Include snacks like toast, rice cakes, or bananas between meals.
5. Watch the Extras
Avoid creamy, fatty sauces or overly oily pizzas that could sit heavily in your stomach. Opt for tomato-based pasta sauces, lean proteins, and simple toppings.
Sample Carb-Loading Day in Bondi
Breakfast: Bagel with scrambled eggs and a side of fruit at Lox Stock & Barrel
Mid-Morning Snack: Slice of banana bread from Sonoma Bakery
Lunch: Wholegrain sandwich with lean turkey, avocado, and a small side salad
Afternoon Snack: Fresh juice and sourdough toast with honey
Dinner: Spaghetti pomodoro at Pompei’s with a bread roll on the side
This approach spreads carbs throughout the day, keeping glycogen topped up without overloading your digestive system.

Carb loading is a key part of marathon success, and in Sydney - especially Bondi - it’s also a culinary experience. From beachside trattorias to artisan bakeries, you’ll find the fuel you need to perform at your best on race day.

Plan your meals, eat smart, and enjoy the process. Because in Bondi, carb loading isn’t just about preparing for 42.2 km - it’s about soaking up one of the world’s most iconic coastal dining scenes before you take on one of its most beautiful marathons.

blocks.text: Discover the best family-friendly things to do in Bondi during Sydney Marathon week - safe swimming spots, playgrounds, cafés, short walks, and rainy-day ideas.

The Sydney Marathon is one of Australia’s premier running events, attracting thousands of participants from around the world. For many runners, it’s also a family affair - partners, children, and friends often travel together, turning race week into a mini holiday. If you’re staying in Sydney with your family, Bondi Beach is the perfect base for pre- and post-race fun.

Just a short trip from the city centre, Bondi offers a mix of kid-friendly beaches, playgrounds, cafés, and easy walks, all wrapped in a laid-back coastal atmosphere. Whether you’re the one running 42.2 km or cheering from the sidelines, you’ll find plenty to keep everyone entertained and happy.
1. Safe Swimming for Kids
Bondi Beach might be famous for its surf, but it also offers calm, shallow spots perfect for little ones.

North Bondi Rock Pool: Located at the northern end of the beach, this shallow, sheltered pool is ideal for young swimmers. It’s protected from waves, with gently sloping entry points and space to splash around. Parents can relax knowing lifeguards are stationed nearby on the main beach.

Bondi Icebergs Children’s Pool: Just below the main Icebergs ocean pool, the kids’ pool is small, shallow, and sheltered from strong currents. It’s a great spot for toddlers and preschoolers to cool off while you enjoy the panoramic coastal view.
Top Tip: Pack hats, rash vests, and reef-safe sunscreen. Sydney’s UV index can be high even in cooler months.
2. Bondi Beach Playground

Right next to the Bondi Pavilion and just metres from the sand, the Bondi Beach playground is a hit with families. It features climbing frames, swings, slides, and shaded seating areas for parents. The location couldn’t be better - you can grab a takeaway coffee from a nearby kiosk and watch your kids play against the backdrop of the ocean.

The playground’s central position also makes it a perfect meeting point if different family members are doing separate activities. Older kids can safely explore the beach or promenade while younger ones enjoy the play equipment.
3. Kid-Friendly Cafés
Bondi’s café scene isn’t just for hip brunch-goers - many venues cater brilliantly to families.
Speedos Café: Known for its colourful smoothie bowls and ocean views, Speedos also offers high chairs, a kids’ menu, and space for prams.
Harry’s Bondi: A relaxed, airy café serving fresh, wholesome meals. Their pancakes and toasties are popular with kids, and staff are welcoming to families.
Porch and Parlour: Slightly more tucked away at North Bondi, this café has a community vibe and is less hectic during peak times.
Pro Tip: Many Bondi cafés get busy on weekends - if you’re visiting after the marathon, aim for an early lunch to avoid queues.
4. Mini Coastal Walks
The famous Bondi to Bronte Coastal Walk is beautiful, but the full route can be a bit much for young kids. The good news is that you can enjoy shorter sections without missing the best scenery.
Bondi to Tamarama: This 1 km stretch is mostly flat with a few gentle inclines and offers stunning views of the cliffs and ocean. Tamarama Beach is small and picturesque, with a café and playground.
North Bondi to Ben Buckler: An easy stroll along the northern headland, with lookouts over the ocean and, in winter, possible whale sightings.
Safety Tip: Always keep young children close on cliff-top paths and avoid the walk in wet or windy conditions.
5. Beach Play Without the Surf

If you’re wary of taking younger kids into the waves, Bondi’s wide sandy expanse is perfect for sandcastle building, kite flying, or a casual game of beach cricket. Bring buckets, spades, and a picnic rug for a relaxed afternoon.
6. Rainy-Day Activities
Even in sunny Sydney, it pays to have a wet-weather plan.
Bondi Pavilion: This heritage building often hosts art workshops, kids’ theatre performances, and community events. Check the schedule during marathon week for family-friendly options.
Bondi Junction Indoor Play Centres: A short bus ride away, Westfield Bondi Junction has indoor play areas and family facilities, making it a good backup plan for rainy days.
Local Libraries: Waverley Library has a great children’s section with books, toys, and occasional storytime sessions.
7. Watching the Sydney Marathon as a Family

If you’re not running, consider heading into the city on race morning to cheer on the runners. The start and finish areas have an electric atmosphere, and kids love holding signs or ringing cowbells to encourage participants.

After the race, head straight to Bondi for a celebratory swim or meal. Public transport from the city is straightforward, with direct buses (333 or 380) or a train-and-bus combination via Bondi Junction.
8. Making the Most of Race Week

Bondi is compact enough to explore without a car, and public transport links make it easy to combine city-based marathon events with beach downtime. If you’re staying in Bondi, you can build your own routine around the race: morning beach play, lunch at a café, an afternoon coastal walk, and early nights to ensure everyone’s rested.
Suggested Family Itinerary for Marathon Week
Day Before the Marathon: Easy morning at the playground, lunch at Harry’s Bondi, afternoon rest at your accommodation, early dinner.
Race Day (if you’re running): Family watches start, heads to Bondi for beach play, meets you post-race for a swim and fish-and-chips dinner.
Day After the Marathon: Sleep in, gentle stroll to Tamarama, brunch at Speedos, afternoon at Bondi Pavilion or Icebergs kids’ pool.

Bondi Beach is more than just an iconic Australian landmark - it’s a place where families can slow down, connect, and create their own marathon-week traditions. From safe swimming spots to scenic walks and rainy-day activities, there’s something for every age and energy level.

So whether your Sydney Marathon trip is about breaking a personal best or simply enjoying time together, Bondi is ready to welcome you with open arms, a wide stretch of sand, and a thousand little moments that will make your family’s visit unforgettable.

blocks.text: Loosen up before the Sydney Marathon with a scenic Bondi Beach shakeout run. Discover easy, scenic routes, sunrise views, and post-run café stops.

With race day looming, you don’t want to tire your legs - but a short, gentle shakeout run can make all the difference to your marathon performance. It helps wake up your muscles, calm your mind, and ease pre-race nerves. In Sydney, there’s no better place for that than Bondi Beach. Famous for its golden sands, ocean breezes, and laid-back vibe, Bondi offers scenic routes that keep things light and easy while giving you a taste of coastal life. Whether you’re a first-time visitor or a returning marathoner, here’s how to make the most of your pre-race shakeout in Bondi.
1. The Classic Bondi Beachfront Jog

The most straightforward shakeout run is the promenade that hugs Bondi Beach from North to South. It’s roughly one kilometre end-to-end, making a 2–3 km out-and-back run effortless to plan. The path is wide, flat, and dotted with water fountains and benches, so you can keep the effort light.
Local tip: Start early in the morning to avoid both the sun and the crowds. The light at sunrise is spectacular, turning the sand a warm gold and the water deep turquoise.
2. Bondi to Bronte Coastal Path

If you want a little more variety, the Bondi to Bronte walk can double as a gentle run. It’s around 3 km each way, but you don’t have to complete the full distance - even a jog to Tamarama Beach and back will give you cliff-top views, ocean spray, and a taste of Sydney’s famous coastal trails.
Watch your step: This path has some uneven sections and stairs, so keep your pace easy to save your legs for race day.
3. Sunrise Shakeout for the Soul

Many visiting runners find it hard to sleep the night before a marathon, especially with jet lag. A sunrise shakeout in Bondi is the perfect way to reset your body clock and mind. Start at North Bondi’s grassy knoll for panoramic views, then cruise along the promenade as the sun breaks the horizon. This isn’t just about running - it’s about grounding yourself in the moment before one of the biggest races of your life.
4. Post-Run Recovery Coffee Stops

Bondi’s café culture is legendary. After your shakeout, reward yourself with a flat white or protein smoothie. Harry’s Bondi is great for healthy bowls, Speedos Café offers hearty breakfast classics, and Cali Press serves up fresh juices to hydrate before race day.
Pro tip: Avoid anything too heavy - the goal is to fuel, not overload, before tomorrow’s effort.
5. Why Bondi is Ideal for a Shakeout
Flat options: Promenade for easy pacing.
Scenic routes: Ocean views boost mental energy.
Facilities: Cafés, toilets, water fountains.
Community vibe: You’ll see plenty of other runners - instant camaraderie.

Your shakeout run should leave you feeling fresh, not fatigued. Bondi’s blend of scenery, atmosphere, and accessible routes make it the perfect pre-marathon playground. So lace up lightly, breathe in the salt air, and enjoy the calm before the marathon storm.

blocks.text: Congratulations! You’ve conquered the Sydney Marathon. Now it’s time to swap running shoes for flip-flops and recover in one of Australia’s most iconic coastal suburbs. Just a short trip from the marathon finish line, Bondi Beach offers everything you need to rest, recharge, and soak up Sydney’s laid-back lifestyle. Here’s your guide to the perfect post-race Bondi experience.
1. Post-Race Recovery Swim Spots

Nothing soothes tired legs like saltwater therapy. Head straight to Bondi Icebergs ocean pool, where cool Pacific waves lap against the pool walls. For something gentler, take a dip in the North Bondi rock pool or venture to nearby Tamarama Beach for a quieter recovery swim. Cold-water immersion can help reduce muscle soreness and speed up recovery.
2. Refuel at Bondi’s Best Cafés

After 42.2km, your body craves quality fuel. Bondi is packed with cafés serving high-protein brunches and fresh smoothies. Try Harry’s Bondi for their legendary green bowls, Lox Stock & Barrel for hearty post-run fare, or Fruitologist for fresh juices and snacks. Don’t forget a flat white – you’ve earned it.
3. Gentle Recovery Walks & Yoga

If your legs are still willing, the Bondi to Bronte Coastal Walk offers breathtaking views without too much strain. For active recovery, book a sunrise yoga class on Bondi Beach – the ocean backdrop and morning light make for a restorative session that’s good for body and mind.
4. Massage & Wellness

Treat yourself to a sports massage at Bondi Junction Remedial Massage or unwind in a float tank at Flow Athletic. For a more indulgent option, check out Koa Recovery, offering infrared saunas and ice baths – perfect for post-race muscle repair.
5. Evening Wind-Down

End the day watching the sun set over the ocean from North Bondi Hill or the Bondi Pavilion promenade. For dinner, choose from casual favourites like Bondi Trattoria or Bills Bondi, where fresh Australian flavours take centre stage.
6. Getting to Bondi After the Marathon

From the marathon finish at the Sydney Opera House, hop on a direct bus (333 or 380) to Bondi Beach, or take the train to Bondi Junction and transfer to a short bus ride. In under 40 minutes, you can be soaking your legs in the surf.
Why Bondi is the Perfect Post-Marathon Destination

With its mix of ocean therapy, healthy dining, wellness options, and spectacular scenery, Bondi Beach is more than just a famous name – it’s the ideal place to recover, celebrate, and reflect on your Sydney Marathon achievement.

blocks.text: Nestled at 211 Bondi Road, Sundays Bondi has become the micro-bakery on every local’s radar-thanks to gooey cinnamon scrolls, dreamy matcha creations and an Instagram strategy that builds FOMO by the minute. If you’re planning a pilgrimage for that first bite, here’s your authoritative guide to the best times to queue-and how to leverage their social channels for insider intel.

Tucked behind a plain façade with no big sign, Sundays Bondi’s discreet storefront only fuels interest - passersby spot a token window and door, then double back when they hear the line snakes around the corner
Know the Official Hours
Their opening hours are Friday - Sunday, 9 am–2 pm (or until sold out).
Peak Times to Queue
On opening weekend, Sundays sold out in one hour-and locals reported the first wave vanishing within 30 minutes . Here’s how to avoid missing out:
Be there before 9am. The very first batch lands at opening, and lines start forming before doors open.
Watch for the 10:30 am “second drop.” They hand-roll and bake in-house, and Instagram Stories usually flash a “Scrolls are back!” alert.
Aim for the final 12pm batch if you can’t make breakfast-though this one moves fast, too.
What to Order

At Sundays Bondi, the cinnamon scroll is the undeniable champion, with its gooey sugar-cinnamon centre and cream-cheese icing snapping up first. Seasonal pistachio scrolls – studded with crunchy nuts and subtly spiced – often sell out by mid-morning, while the cardamom-infused variation has become a cult hit. For matcha lovers, the vibrant matcha scroll and silky matcha latte rank among top-sellers, especially when paired as the ultimate Green Tea Duo. Limited-edition flavours such as salted caramel and white chocolate-macadamia debut monthly, generating FOMO-fuelled queues. Whether classic or creative, these fan favourites define the Sundays Bondi experience and constant Instagram hype.
Insider Tips from the Locals
Follow them on Instagram to vote on next flavours. Monthly scroll-flavour polls in Stories often let followers choose upcoming specials.
Tag #SundaysBondi. User-generated posts can get featured-and occasionally rewarded with free scrolls.
Go takeaway & roam. With limited seating, grab your order to go and enjoy it on the promenade or in the sand.
Ask for extra icing, or request an off-menu swirl twist-they often accommodate friendly asks.
How to Get to Sundays Bondi: Public Transport & Parking

Located at 211 Bondi Road, Sundays Bondi is just a short stroll from Bondi Junction station. Catch the 333 bus from Circular Quay or the 324 from the CBD-both stop right outside the bakery. If you’re driving, street parking is metered Mon–Sun (8 am–8 pm) on Bondi Road and side streets; aim for a spot on Brighton Blvd or Blair Street for free parking after 2 pm on weekends. Rideshares and bike racks are also plentiful, making it easy to swing by for scrolls without the stress of finding a car park.
Small-Batch Baking & Surprise Flavours

Founder Laetitia Loefti rolls the dough in-house, keeping batches small to maximise freshness. Instagram teasers hint at rotating specials-think Kinder Bueno matcha scrolls or monthly Biscoff drops-that sell out within minutes of a “Scrolls are back!” Story alert .
Pricing That Reflects Premium Ingredients

Expect to pay $9 for a classic cream-cheese scroll or $9.50 for a flavoured version, with matcha drinks from $8–$11. These prices underscore the use of single-origin cinnamon, ceremonial-grade matcha and locally sourced dairy for that signature ooze and silky froth

Whether you’re after your first sugar-cinnamon fix or chasing the month’s mystery scroll flavour, planning around these insider insights will put you at the front of the queue. Follow their Instagram for real-time drops, show up right at 9 am, and you’ll be sinking teeth into Bondi’s most coveted cinnamon scroll before anyone else. Enjoy the ritual.

Bondi Beach isn’t just famous for its waves and sand-it’s a mecca for coffee lovers. After scouring review platforms, local guides, and on-the-ground visits, we’ve distilled the essentials into a definitive ranking from #10 to #1. Whether you crave a beachside flat white, experimental brews, or roastery-fresh espresso, this list-backed by Visit Bondi Beach, Urban List, Broadsheet, and TripAdvisor-will steer you toward Bondi’s best caffeine fixes.
10. Bill’s
79 Hall Street, Bondi Beach

Bill Granger’s beloved Sydney institution landed at Bondi in 2014, marrying airy interiors with reliably delicious coffee-typically Campos beans-and classic brunch fare. Beyond its fluffy scrambled eggs and ricotta hotcakes, Bill’s offers a consistently well-balanced flat white that’s smooth, slightly creamy, and never over-extracted. Perfect for tourists seeking a taste of Sydney’s café heritage, it’s also a solid fallback on busy weekends when locals flock elsewhere.
9. Glory Days
Bondi Pavilion, Queen Elizabeth Drive, Bondi Beach

Nestled in the iconic Pavilion, Glory Days pairs beachfront views with thoughtfully roasted beans (The Good Atelier supply), delivering bright, clean cups that cut through Bondi sun haze. While famous for breakfast burritos and açai bowls, the coffee here-whether an early morning flat white or an afternoon long black-consistently earns praise for its clarity and balance. Pro tip: grab your order and claim a lounger on the sand.
8. Harry’s Bondi
2/136 Wairoa Avenue, Bondi Beach

Formerly a no-frills espresso bar, Harry’s now dazzles with both inventive “H” canned matchas and expertly pulled espressos using single-origin beans sourced in collaboration with top roasteries. Amid prawn omelettes and croissants, the coffee program shines-expect rich crema, balanced acidity, and a smoother-than-average texture. The rotating lineup of dairy-free smoothies doesn’t hurt, but it’s the house-espresso that keeps true coffee aficionados coming back.
7. Speedos Café
126 Ramsgate Avenue, North Bondi

Billed as Bondi’s most Instagrammable café, Speedos serves more than just picture-perfect pancake towers. Their coffee menu-featuring locally roasted beans-delivers a punchy espresso with dark-chocolate notes and lingering sweetness, ideal for cutting through colourful smoothie bowls. The ocean views from the window bench elevate any caffeine hit, making it a coveted spot for sunset lattes and dawn-till-dusk brew sessions.
6. Pocket
266 Campbell Parade, Bondi Beach

From the Makaveli team, Pocket pairs its stellar brunch plates with an equally impressive coffee program. They source beans from boutique Sydney roasteries and pull shots with precision-expect caramel-sweet notes framed by a velvety mouthfeel. Whether you opt for a classic cappuccino or an off-menu batch brew, the coffee here matches the food’s quality and the café’s chic corner-spot ambiance.
5. Chapter One
34 Campbell Parade, Bondi Beach

Opposite the waves, Chapter One has been a Bondi staple since 2012. Their coffee-blended in-house with house-roasted and local single-origin beans-strikes a harmonious balance of brightness and body. Regulars praise the consistency of their flat whites and cortados, even during peak brunch hours. Pair your cup with one of their gourmet bagels or organic açai bowls for a quintessential Bondi morning.
4. Makaveli
177, 2/179 Glenayr Avenue, Bondi Beach

This day-to-night hotspot turns heads with its chilli-tequila espresso martini, but morning coffee reigns supreme. Makaveli sources custom roasts from Brickfields, resulting in shots with pronounced chocolate undertones and a subtle berry finish. The laid-back interior invites you to linger over your brew-ideal for before or after the weekly pasta nights and bottomless brunches that fill locals’ calendars.
3. Blackwood
Shop 3/87–89 Glenayr Avenue, Bondi Beach

Blackwood brings Michelin-trained finesse to Bondi’s café scene. Their coffee-often a signature biscoff latte or coconut-lychee matcha-is crafted from premium single-origins, showcasing bright, fruity acidity balanced by creamy sweetness. Arrive early to snag a window seat and taste the famed truffled chilli scrambled eggs alongside a flawlessly executed espresso. It’s a gourmet experience from bean to bite.
2. Coffee Bondi Beach
Shop 1, 128 Campbell Parade, Bondi Beach

Housed in a 100-year-old space, this roastery-café from Brooklands founders Cam Price and Joe Pags champions vegan and sustainable practices. Their single-origin pour-overs highlight distinct tasting notes-think delicate florals or rich praline-while baristas guide you through brewing techniques. With behind-the-scenes roastery tours available most mornings, it’s both an educational and sensory coffee pilgrimage.
1. Will & Co
HQ Tasting Bar, 29–31 Derby Street, Bondi Beach

Crowned Bondi’s ultimate coffee destination, Will & Co is a micro-roastery, barista training hub, and tasting bar rolled into one. Every cup-whether a meticulously dialed espresso or signature batch brew-is handled with obsessive precision. Expect full-bodied shots with toffee sweetness and clean finishes. The tasting bar offers rotating single-origin flights, making it a must for coffee purists and curious visitors alike.
Insider Tips for Coffee Lovers
Beat the crowds: Visit off-peak (weekdays before 8 am or after 2 pm).
Bring reusables: Many shops offer discounts for your own cup.
Ask for recommendations: Local baristas love to share their current favourite single-origin pour.

blocks.text: The Bondi to Bronte Swim is one of Australia’s most beloved ocean swimming events, attracting thousands each summer. Whether you’re a first-time open water swimmer or a casual athlete looking for a new challenge, this guide breaks down everything you need to know to take the plunge with confidence.
What Is the Bondi to Bronte Swim?

The Bondi to Bronte Ocean Swim is a 2.1 km point-to-point open water race held each December. It starts at Sydney’s famous Bondi Beach and finishes at Bronte Beach, passing stunning coastal scenery and rolling swells.
Distance: 2.1 km
Typical Conditions: Ocean swells, rips, and possible chop
Date: Early December each year
Organised by: Bronte Surf Life Saving Club
Course Overview

The swim starts at the south end of Bondi Beach, heading past McKenzie’s Point, following the coastline, and finishing at Bronte Beach. You’ll be swimming over reefs, through deep water, and into Bronte’s surf zone.
Tip: Expect challenging water. It’s a “proper” ocean swim, not a flat-water race.
What You’ll Need
Goggles – Preferably tinted for glare
Wetsuit (optional) – The water can be cold; most swimmers go without
Swim cap – Provided with your wave pack
Timing chip – Issued at registration
Pre-race nutrition – Light meal 90 minutes before
Registration & Categories
Entry fee: ~$60–$80
Categories: Based on age and gender, plus elite divisions
Mini Swim: A shorter course (approx. 800m) for juniors and novices
Online registration: Opens around September via bonditobronte.com.au
How to Train as a Beginner
Ocean swimming is very different from the pool. Here’s a basic plan:
4–6 Weeks Out
Swim 2–3 times per week
Include interval training in the pool (e.g. 4×400m)
Add one ocean swim per week, if possible
2 Weeks Out
Do at least one 1.5–2 km continuous ocean swim
Practice sighting and swimming straight in open water
Race Week
Taper with lighter swims
Rest well and eat clean
Consider joining a swim squad like BondiFit or attending local surf club ocean swim sessions.
Race Day Tips for First-Timers
Arrive early: Parking fills quickly-use public transport or walk
Warm up: Swim 100–200m beforehand
Stay calm: Start wide to avoid the mid-pack scramble
Sight often: Aim for the buoys and keep McKenzie’s Point on your left
Finish strong: Watch for rips at Bronte-stay between the flags
Is It Safe?
Yes-with a few caveats. The event is professionally managed, with dozens of surf lifesavers and rescue craft on the course. Still, it’s essential you:
Can swim 2 km confidently in open water
Know basic surf safety
Understand how to float and call for help
Spectator Info
Bronte Beach is the perfect vantage point. Bring a picnic and watch the action from the grassy hill or surf club. The finish line has food, drinks, and live commentary.
FAQ
Do I need to be super fit?
No-but you must be able to swim 2 km confidently without breaks.
What’s the water temperature?
Usually 17–21°C in December.
Are flippers or snorkels allowed?
No. Standard swimming gear only.
Can I enter on race day?
Not usually. It sells out-register early.
The Bondi to Bronte Swim is a rite of passage for ocean lovers and endurance seekers alike. With the right prep and mindset, it’s a challenge any confident swimmer can conquer.

blocks.text: Let’s be real. The name alone is intimidating.

Heartbreak Hill is the most feared part of Sydney’s iconic City2Surf fun run - a 2km steady uphill from Rose Bay to Vaucluse that hits just as your legs are wondering why you signed up for this in the first place.
But here’s the truth: you don’t need to be fit, fast or fancy to finish it. You just need a simple plan, a few habits, and some good old Aussie stubbornness.
In this guide, you’ll get an easy 8-week training plan that even self-confessed couch potatoes can follow. It’s fun, flexible, and made for real people - not gym junkies.
First, What Is Heartbreak Hill?

It’s a 2km uphill stretch that starts around kilometre 6 of the 14km City2Surf course. It’s not a steep sprint - more of a long, draining climb that tests your endurance and mental grit. If you’ve done no hill training, it can feel like forever. If you’ve prepped just a little? You’ll fly.
Who This Plan Is For
You’re a beginner (or haven’t run since high school)
You want to walk-jog City2Surf, not sprint it
You’re nervous about Heartbreak Hill
You like casual exercise, not full-blown training mode
8-Week Beginner Plan to Tackle Heartbreak Hill
Each week builds up slowly. You’ll start with easy walk-jogs, introduce gentle hill walks, add a little strength, and finish feeling proud - not broken.
Week 1–2: Build the Habit
You’re just getting moving. Focus on frequency, not intensity.
Tuesdays – 2–3km walk-jog (run 30 sec, walk 90 sec - repeat)
Wednesdays – Gentle hill walk (find a 1–2 minute hill, walk up 3–4 times)
Fridays – Bodyweight strength: 10 squats, 10 lunges each leg, 20 sec plank
Saturdays – Long walk-jog (start with 4km; walk when needed)
👉 Goal: Move 4–5 days per week. Nothing fancy - just show up.
Week 3–4: Start Climbing
Time to train your legs and lungs for that hill. Keep building slowly.
Tuesdays – 3–4km walk-jog (increase running intervals to 1 min jog / 1 min walk)
Wednesdays – Hill intervals: walk up a gentle hill 4–5 times, jog down slowly
Fridays – Strength + step-ups (10 each leg on a park bench)
Saturdays – Long walk-jog (5–6km). Try to include one hill if you can
👉 Goal: Get used to hills and longer time on your feet.
Week 5–6: Get Comfortable Being Uncomfortable
The mid-point. You’re getting stronger, so we gently push the limits.
Tuesdays – 4–5km jog-walk (2 min jog / 1 min walk)
Wednesdays – Hill repeats: 6× 60–90 sec uphill (walk or jog)
Fridays – Strength: 2 rounds of your basic bodyweight set
Saturdays – 7–8km long walk-jog. Include some hills, even small ones
👉 Goal: Build mental toughness and learn to keep going when it gets hard.
Week 7: Practice the Hill
You’re nearly ready. This is the week to get a feel for Heartbreak Hill itself if you can.
Tuesdays – 5km jog-walk (3 min jog / 1 min walk)
Wednesdays – Optional: walk/run up the actual Heartbreak Hill (from Rose Bay to Vaucluse)
Fridays – Strength + mobility (foam rolling, stretching)
Saturdays – 9–10km walk-jog. Try the full City2Surf route if you’re up for it
👉 Goal: Build confidence on real hills. You’re stronger than you think.
Week 8: Taper & Trust Yourself
Race week! Cut back, keep moving, and don’t do anything silly.
Tuesday – Easy 3km jog or walk
Thursday – Short 15-min walk or stretch
Sunday – Race day! Show up, smile, and enjoy the crowd
👉 Goal: Start slow, walk the hill if needed, and soak in the energy.
Where to Train Hills in Sydney
Lyne Park, Rose Bay – perfect starter hill
Centennial Park – rolling terrain, ideal for jogs and long walks
Bondi to Bronte coastal walk – stunning, slightly hilly, and not boring
The 15-Minute Strength Set (2× a Week)
No gym required. Just use your body.
10 squats
10 lunges per leg
30-second plank
10 step-ups (park bench or stair)
Optional: light stretch or foam roll afterward
👉 Strong legs = less pain on hills.
Race Day Tips for Heartbreak Hill
Start slow – the hill is at km 6… don’t burn out at km 2
Take walk breaks – it’s a fun run, not the Olympics
Breathe deep, swing your arms – rhythm helps
Use the crowd – they’ll cheer you up the hill
Smile at the top – it’s mostly downhill after that
Final Pep Talk
You don’t need to run the whole thing. You don’t need to crush a PB. You just need to show up, keep moving, and remember that walking is perfectly allowed - and often smart.
Heartbreak Hill might look scary on a map, but with 8 weeks of gentle training, you’ll be ready to meet it head-on. Good luck!

blocks.text: Moving to Australia for work or travel promises sun-drenched beaches, vibrant cities, and endless opportunities Down Under. However, navigating the initial hurdles-from securing the right visa to mastering cost-saving tricks-can feel overwhelming. Whether you’re on a Working Holiday visa or planning a permanent move, careful planning and insider insights will help you settle comfortably while stretching your budget. This comprehensive guide delivers 25 essential, research-backed hacks-incorporating top tips from our featured image like opening a Westpac account, snagging an AldiMobile SIM, and browsing Facebook Marketplace-to streamline your transition. You’ll learn how to minimize fees, optimize transport, secure healthcare and superannuation, and network with locals. Ready to fast-track your Aussie adventure? Follow these practical, actionable strategies to start a new life in Australia smoothly and confidently, and embrace the local culture faster than you ever thought possible.
25 Essential Hacks
1. Choose the right visa
Compare Working Holiday (417/462), Skilled Migrant, and Student visas; match your goals, budget, eligibility, and health-cover needs.
2. Pre-arrival document checklist
Gather passports, birth certificates, academic transcripts, immunisation records, and character references; store digital copies in secure cloud storage for swift processing.
3. Obtain a Tax File Number
Apply for your TFN online via the Australian Taxation Office before your first payday to reduce withholding and avoid payroll delays.
4. Open a Westpac bank account
Use Westpac’s Breeze account for fee-free first year and user-friendly transfers; verify identity online before you land.
5. Set up a Wise borderless account
Transfer funds at mid-market exchange rates; lock in favorable rates and access multi-currency holdings with minimal fees.
6. Purchase an AldiMobile SIM
Grab a prepaid SIM on the Telstra network for nationwide coverage and budget-friendly data plans starting under $10 per month.
7. Load your Opal/Myki/Go Card
Preload transport cards in Sydney, Melbourne, or Brisbane; use apps and auto top-up to avoid fines and unlock daily fare caps.
8. Bookmark local transport apps
Download TripView, Moovit, and Uber for real-time schedules, route planning, and cheap rideshares during off-peak hours.
9. Book short-term stays
Secure initial lodging via Airbnb, Hostelworld, or Stayz; negotiate weekly discounts to keep costs low while scouting neighbourhoods.
10. Find long-term rentals via share platforms
Use Flatmates.com.au, Gumtree, and Facebook groups to split rent with roommates and access furnished houses quickly.
11. Unlock second-hand deals
Shop Facebook Marketplace, Gumtree, and Cash Converters for furniture, appliances, and electronics; always inspect items in person before purchasing.
12. Shop groceries at Aldi
Fill your trolley with Aldi’s budget-friendly basics and weekly specials, then compare Coles and Woolworths promotions for extra savings.
13. Use grocery-deal apps
Install Price Hipster, ShopFully, or the Coles and Woolworths apps to track loyalty rewards, digital coupons, and flash markdowns.
14. Compare petrol prices
Use FuelMap, PetrolSpy, and MotorMouth apps to find the cheapest nearby pumps; fill up before weekends to avoid surcharges.
15. Secure healthcare cover
Check your visa’s Medicare eligibility under reciprocal agreements, or buy private health insurance via Bupa, NIB, or Medibank.
16. Register for Medicare (if eligible)
Once your visa qualifies, enrol online for a Medicare card to access bulk-billed services and reduced hospital costs.
17. Apply for an ABN for side gigs
Freelancers and gig workers must register an Australian Business Number; invoice clients and track GST obligations.
18. Set up superannuation
Ask your employer to contribute to funds like Hostplus or AustralianSuper; review fees and investment options for long-term growth.
19. Understand pay rates and awards
Consult the Fair Work Ombudsman website to verify your industry’s minimum pay, penalty rates, and workplace rights.
20. Use local job platforms
Create alerts on Seek, Indeed, and LinkedIn; tailor your resume to Australian standards and network via professional groups.
21. Network at free events
Attend Meetups, Internations, and community workshops; join hobby clubs and sports teams to build friendships and local connections.
22. Convert your driver’s license
Check your state’s transport authority for reciprocal agreements and apply to swap your foreign license without retaking tests.
23. Budget with finance apps
Track spending and set savings goals using Pocketbook, MoneyBrilliant, or Frollo; sync your Aussie bank accounts for real-time insights.
24. Manage services with MyGov
Link ATO, Medicare, Centrelink, and child-support through a single MyGov account; enable two-factor authentication for security.
25. Join expat communities
Follow Australia Working Holiday, Expat Forum, and r/australia threads on Reddit and Facebook for up-to-date tips, job leads, and meet-ups.

Moving abroad is as much about mindset as it is about logistics. By following these 25 hacks-from setting up key services to leveraging budget apps and local networks-you’ll accelerate your adaptation and focus on what matters: enjoying Australia’s unique lifestyle, culture, and career opportunities. Remember to stay flexible, keep an eye on local regulations, and tweak your strategy as you gain experience. Bookmark this guide, revisit the tips regularly, and join expat communities to stay updated. With the right preparation and these insider tricks in your toolkit, your transition to life in Australia will be smoother, more affordable, and infinitely more rewarding.

title: Tamarama, Coogee & Clovelly Parking Guide
metaDescription: Where to park at Tamarama, Coogee and Clovelly - free and paid spots, time limits and local tips for the Eastern Beaches south of Bondi.
h1: Tamarama, Coogee & Clovelly Beach Parking: Ultimate Guide to Free & Paid Spots
intro: Tamarama, Coogee & Clovelly Beach Parking: Ultimate Guide to Free & Paid Spots — Visit Bondi Beach Visit Bondi Beach Bondi Beach Guide What's On Swim Accommodation Tours Bondi Icebergs Gallery About Bondi Beach Guide What's On Swim Accommodation Tours Bondi Icebergs Gallery About Visit Bondi Beach Tamarama, Coogee & Clovelly Beach Parking: Ultimate Guide to Free & Paid Spots Parking near Sydney’s eastern suburbs beaches-Tamarama, Coogee, and Clovelly-can be challenging, especially

blocks.text: Parking near Sydney’s eastern suburbs beaches-Tamarama, Coogee, and Clovelly-can be challenging, especially on weekends and during summer. Below is a concise, fully verified guide to on-street and off-street parking options, restrictions, and free bays for each beach. Wherever specific details (such as exact rates or street names) could not be confirmed, they have been omitted to ensure accuracy.
Tamarama Beach

Tamarama Beach has very limited on-street parking. In fact, Waverley Council explicitly advises that there is only “limited on-street parking” near Tamarama and recommends using public transport where possible .

On-Street Parking All available parking is on local streets adjacent to Tamarama Park (Tamarama Marine Drive area). These bays are unrestricted in terms of payment (i.e., no meters), but they fill extremely quickly, particularly on weekends and holidays . Time Restrictions: Parking signage in Tamarama generally indicates a 2-hour limit (2P) between 8 am and 6 pm, seven days a week, for most on-street bays in Waverley Council beach precincts (including Tamarama) . Outside those hours, parking is unrestricted-but bays are still limited. Off-Street/Public Transport There is no Council-operated off-street public car park immediately servicing Tamarama Beach. The large nearby lots (e.g., Hollywood Avenue Car Park or Bondi Beach lots) are several hundred metres away and intended for residents or Bondi visitors . Insider Tip: Waverley Council recommends using the 378 bus (Bondi Junction ↔ Tamarama) or walking from Bondi Beach (about 1 km north) or Bronte Beach (about 700 m south) via the Coastal Walk, rather than searching for street parking.
Coogee Beach
Coogee Beach falls under Randwick Council, which introduced a 4-hour time limit (4P) on all on-street bays in its beachside precincts (including Coogee and Clovelly) as of January 2021 .
On-Street Parking (Free, 4P Limit)
All street-side bays within approximately 500 m of Coogee Beach are free to use but strictly limited to 4 hours maximum (4P) at any time .

Outside those 4 hours, standard NSW road rules apply (e.g., you must not park in tow-away zones, driveway crossovers, or no-parking areas). There are no pay-and-display meters for most on-street bays-just the 4 hour restriction. Insider Tip: On busy summer weekends, expect on-street bays to be full by 10 am. If you can’t find a spot within 300 m of the beach, consider parking farther up Beach Street or Brook Street (still within 4P zones) and walking the final 5–10 minutes . Randwick Council Car Parks (Paid; PayStay App)

Coogee Beach Car Park: Located adjacent to the southern end of Coogee Beach (at the corner of Beach Street and Arden Street). This Council-managed lot is metered and uses PayStay smart-parking technology-drivers can pay by coin, card, or the PayStay app, and view real-time availability via digital signs. Payment: Pay-and-display is obsolete; all sessions are managed via PayStay. Rates are set by Randwick Council (exact hourly rates vary by season). Coogee Oval Car Park: Slightly inland on Brook Street, near Coogee Oval. Also meter-controlled via PayStay, with real-time availability signage . Insider Tip: Use PayStay’s “nearby” function to check if spaces are available before driving into the car park. Private Off-Street Option

Care Park – Coogee Bay Village Car Park: Located at 196 Coogee Bay Road (the southern end of Coogee Bay Village shopping complex). Open daily from 6 am to midnight; hourly rates start at $9/hr for the first hour, with a maximum daily rate of $30. Monthly packages are also available . Insider Tip: If Council car parks are full, Care Park is a reliable paid alternative just a 2 minute walk from Coogee Beach.
Clovelly Beach
Clovelly Beach is likewise under Randwick Council, with both free on-street parking (4 hour limit) and a large free public lot adjacent to Bundock Park.
Off-Street, Free Car Park (Bundock Park)
Bundock Park Car Park: Located at 3–25 Eastbourne Avenue, Clovelly. It offers approximately 100 spaces (exact count unspecified, but substantial) and is free at all times .
Restrictions: Bundock Park is within the 4 hour limit zone between 8 am and 6 pm-so if you exceed 4 hours, you risk a fine. Outside those times, parking is unrestricted.
Insider Tip: On weekends, the Bundock Park lot fills by around 10 am. If full, try Clovelly Road (on-street) or Victory Street, but watch for 4P signage.
On-Street Parking (Free, 4P Limit)
Surrounding streets (Clovelly Road, Victory Street, Tramless Lane, etc.) have free on-street bays subject to 4 hour maximum from 8 am to 6 pm .
Outside the 4 hour window (before 8 am & after 6 pm), street parking is unrestricted but remains limited in supply.

Insider Tip: If Bundock Park is full and you don’t mind a short stroll, park near Coogee Beach (where parking may be slightly more available) and follow the Coastal Walk north to Clovelly (about 15 minutes).
Summary
Tamarama Beach: Only very limited free on-street bays (2 hour limit) and no public off-street lot. Best to use public transport or walk via the Coastal Walk from Bondi or Bronte .
Coogee Beach: Free on-street (4 hour limit), two Council car parks (metered via PayStay), and a private Care Park lot nearby. Arrive early or use PayStay to check availability .
Clovelly Beach: Free Bundock Park lot (4 hour limit) plus free on-street bays (4 hour limit). If full, consider walking from Coogee or deeper residential streets .

Timing is critical: on sunny weekends and holidays, most free bays (especially Bundock Park at Clovelly or street bays near Coogee) are gone by 10 am. Always check the posted 2P/4P signage, use apps like PayStay for real-time updates, and consider public transport as a reliable alternative to circling for a space.

title: Sydney Airport Taxi Scams: How to Spot and Avoid Them
metaDescription: How to spot and avoid taxi scams at Sydney Airport - the common rip-offs, your rights and cheaper, safer ways to get to Bondi.
h1: Sydney Airport Taxi Scams: How to Spot & Avoid Costly Rip-Offs for a Hassle-Free Arrival
intro: Sydney Airport Taxi Scams: How to Spot & Avoid Costly Rip-Offs for a Hassle-Free Arrival — Visit Bondi Beach Visit Bondi Beach Bondi Beach Guide What's On Swim Accommodation Tours Bondi Icebergs Gallery About Bondi Beach Guide What's On Swim Accommodation Tours Bondi Icebergs Gallery About Visit Bondi Beach Sydney Airport Taxi Scams: How to Spot & Avoid Costly Rip-Offs for a Hassle-Free Arrival Arriving at Sydney Airport should mark the exciting start of your Australian adventure, but

blocks.text: Arriving at Sydney Airport should mark the exciting start of your Australian adventure, but a handful of taxi scams can leave travellers out of pocket before they even reach their destination. Familiarising yourself with these common tactics and knowing how to avoid them will help ensure a smooth, stress-free journey. Below, you’ll find descriptions of the most prevalent taxi scams at Sydney Airport-each with practical advice on spotting and steering clear of them.
Whilst not the cheapest option, if catching a taxi is a concern, private transfers can provide extra peace of mind. You can check out Kiwi Taxis as one such option: https://kiwitaxi.tp.st/Bxy9XEGl
1. Unlicensed or “Gypsy” Taxis

Many travellers think they’re jumping into an official taxi, only to find they’re in an unlicensed vehicle operated by a driver who may overcharge, take a longer route, or even drive dangerously. These drivers often wait just outside the official taxi ranks, touting loudly: “Taxi? Taxi? Lower fare!” or “I can get you there cheaper!” Although it can be tempting to save a few dollars, these vehicles are not regulated by Transport for NSW-meaning there’s no assurance of proper insurance coverage, driver background checks, or calibrated meters.
How to avoid it:
Always queue at the official taxi rank inside the airport terminal. Signs will direct you to “Taxis” on the arrivals level.
Don’t accept offers from drivers approaching you outside the sanctioned zones. Politely decline and head for the designated rank.
Look for the NSW Taxi Plate displayed prominently on the windscreen and the taxi roof sign with an illuminated “TAXI” light.
By insisting on an official taxi, you protect yourself against safety risks and surprise bills.
2. Refusal to Use the Meter

A common ploy is for a driver to claim their meter is broken or “won’t accept credit cards,” then quote you a high flat rate. This tactic leaves you vulnerable to inflated fares, especially if you’re unfamiliar with the approximate distance or typical cost to your hotel or accommodation.
How to avoid it:
Politely insist that the driver switch on the meter. Under NSW regulations, all licensed taxis must run by meter unless you agree on a pre‐calculated “set fare.”
If they refuse, exit immediately and find another taxi at the official rank. Never board a taxi that won’t use its meter.
If you prepaid via a ride-booking app (e.g., 13Cabs or Silver Service), you should have a digital booking reference that guarantees a set fare.
Keep in mind that an official meter fare is transparent and regulated. Always double-check the meter before the journey begins.
3. Taking an Unnecessarily Long Route

Some drivers take advantage of distracted or jet-lagged passengers by looping around circular routes, driving through expensive toll roads, or detouring into congested areas-thus padding the fare. Even if the meter ticks up gradually, those extra kilometres can translate into a surprisingly high final bill.
How to avoid it:
Before getting in, check your destination on Google Maps or another navigation app so you know the most direct route.
Politely monitor the GPS path on your phone during the trip. If the driver deviates significantly, gently question them (“Is this route faster?”).

For an added layer of protection, request a receipt at the end of your trip and note the total distance and time. If something seems off, you can lodge a complaint with NSW Fair Trading or the taxi operator.
Being familiar with Sydney’s road layout and having basic navigation tools on hand will deter drivers from veering off the sensible route.
4. Hidden Airport Surcharges and Additional Fees

Sydney Airport taxis are entitled to charge a regulated airport pick-up fee (currently around $4–$5 AUD) and a late-night surcharge. While these are legitimate, some drivers tack on extra “handling” fees or claim baggage will cost additional flat rates - sometimes double-charging you.
How to avoid it:
Check the official Transport for NSW taxi fare schedule online (via transport.nsw.gov.au) so you know the regulated surcharges:
Airport pick-up fee (automatically added when the meter is switched on inside the airport).
Late-night surcharge (for trips starting or ending between specified hours).
Refuse any unsolicited “baggage handling” fees-official taxis do not charge separately for standard luggage unless it requires special handling (e.g., oversized items).

Confirm surcharges before getting in: ask the driver, “Are there any airport pick-up or late-night fees applied?” If they cannot explain these transparently, consider exiting and choosing another cab.
Transparency is your ally-being aware of regulated surcharges prevents a driver from inventing bogus fees.
5. Prepaid Taxi Booth Rip-Offs

Sydney Airport houses official taxi booking booths where travellers can prepay for “scratch tickets” or arranged taxi services. Occasionally, inexperienced visitors buy tickets from unofficial kiosks or booking agents situated just outside the arrivals hall or in nearby shops-only to discover their ticket is worthless or “invalid,” forcing them to pay again.
How to avoid it:
Only purchase prepaid taxi tickets from the official booking booths inside the terminal (clearly marked as run by Sydney Airport).
If in doubt, walk a few extra steps toward the taxi rank: there will be official counters with consistent signage (yellow “Taxi” logo on black).
Avoid touts or independent agents claiming they can book a cheaper taxi service. In most cases, a metered taxi from the airport rank will be comparable in price and more reliable.
By buying tickets solely from the sanctioned booths, you ensure the driver must accept your voucher and collect you directly from the rank-no unexpected fees or invalid tickets.
6. Overpriced Fixed-Fare Offers from Private Drivers

Immediately outside the arrival gates, some private drivers displaying signs for “cheap ride to CBD” or “fixed fare to Bondi” may offer flat rates that seem attractive, especially to budget travellers who don’t own data to check typical taxi fares. In reality, these flat rates sometimes exceed what a metered taxi would cost-plus they bypass regulated channels, leaving no easy recourse if something goes wrong.
How to avoid it:
Politely decline offers from drivers not affiliated with a registered taxi company.
If you prefer a flat rate, use a reputable ride-booking platform (e.g., Uber, Ola, DiDi) where the fare is calculated upfront, and you can compare costs.
Always compare the quoted flat fare with a quick Google search or a taxi from the official rank, which will usually charge you less or roughly the same.
Comparing options in real-time (even a quick glance at your phone) prevents overpaying for a seemingly “bargain” fixed fare.
7. False “Credit Card Terminal Issues”

Some scam drivers claim they cannot process credit cards because “the terminal is broken” or “the bank machine at the airport won’t communicate.” They then demand cash upfront or inflate the fare once you’re in the car. Occasionally, they’ll produce a visibly old machine with disconnected cables, hoping you won’t notice until the end of the trip.
How to avoid it:
Before getting in, ask whether credit cards are accepted. Genuine taxi meters in Sydney are almost always equipped with working EFTPOS terminals.
If the driver insists they can’t take cards, politely refuse and exit the taxi. Legitimate drivers won’t hesitate to process a card payment.
Carry some Australian dollars to cover small fares, but if you must pay cash, request a printed receipt and note the driver’s details for future follow-up.
A driver who truly can’t process cards must still let you exit-never feel pressured to hand over cash for a ride you haven’t yet taken.
Final Tips
Taxi scams at Sydney Airport aren’t widespread, but a handful of unscrupulous operators prey on weary or distracted travellers. To safeguard yourself:
Stick to official taxi ranks inside the terminal.
Insist on using the meter-refuse flat-rate or “meter broken” excuses.
Familiarise yourself with regulated airport surcharges so you can identify bogus fees.
Compare flat-fare offers to metered taxi rates via a quick online check.
Verify that the driver accepts cards before starting your journey.

If you ever feel unsafe or suspect foul play, exit the vehicle immediately and report the driver to the airport’s Taxi Customer Service or call NSW Fair Trading at 13 32 20. By staying alert, doing a little pre-trip research, and relying on official channels, you can enjoy Sydney without falling victim to airport taxi scams.

blocks.text: Bondi Beach is world-famous - and with good reason. But beyond the iconic surf, sunbathers, and cafés lies a local side to Bondi that’s full of surprises. If you want to explore Bondi like a local, here are 10 hidden gems that offer something truly unique - whether you’re chasing ocean views, secret snacks, or serene escapes.
1. Gould Street’s Independent Boutiques

Just a block back from the beach, Gould Street is a haven for fashion lovers. Lined with stylish Australian labels, eco-conscious brands, and minimalist design stores, it’s where the locals go for retail therapy - minus the tourist buzz.
Tip: Visit in the late morning to browse peacefully before the lunch rush.
2. Ben Buckler Point

At the northern tip of Bondi, Ben Buckler offers a rugged, rocky viewpoint ideal for sunrise, sea watching, or quiet reflection. It’s also home to a historic WWII bunker and panoramic views of the Pacific Ocean, all hidden in plain sight.
3. Bondi Wash Flagship Store

Inspired by native Australian botanicals, Bondi Wash sells luxurious, plant-based home and body products. Their flagship boutique on Gould Street is beautifully curated - and you’ll leave smelling amazing.
Look for their exclusive Bondi scent - a subtle nod to the sea breeze and coastal flora.
4. Speedos Café (Early Hours Secret)

Speedos is no secret, but here’s the trick: visit before 9am on a weekday. You’ll find a peaceful pocket of Bondi life - locals sipping green smoothies, watching surfers, and soaking in the morning sun. Their vegan pancakes and smoothie bowls are legendary.
5. Ray O’Keefe Reserve & Hidden Tide Pool
Located just above the North Bondi rocks, this peaceful green space has a hidden natural tide pool perfect for a quiet dip. Ideal for families or anyone seeking a more tranquil swim.
Bring a book and a towel - it’s a great spot for a lazy afternoon.
6. Sculptures That Stay

Bondi’s famous Sculpture by the Sea event may only happen once a year, but several public artworks remain all year round. Wander the coastal walk slowly and you’ll spot wave-shaped sculptures, sandstone art, and ocean-inspired installations that many miss.
7. Bondi Road Community Garden

Hidden between buildings on Bondi Road lies a lush community garden where locals grow herbs, veggies, and native plants. It’s open to the public, and offers a welcome moment of calm and greenery in the middle of the buzz.
8. Porch and Parlour’s Off-Menu Toastie

Porch and Parlour is a Bondi institution, but here’s a hot tip: there’s an off-menu toastie that regulars quietly order - crispy, cheesy, and utterly delicious. Ask with a smile, and you might just be in on the secret.
9. Backstreet Street Art Trails

Venture off the main roads and into the laneways behind Hall Street and Curlewis Street to discover Bondi’s vibrant and ever-changing street art. Look out for the famous “It’s Okay to Not Be Okay” mural - and don’t forget your camera.
10. Bondi Icebergs Sauna & Recovery Zone

You’ve seen the pool in postcards - but did you know that Bondi Icebergs also offers a public-access sauna and recovery area? It’s the ultimate post-run or post-surf experience, and far less crowded than the pool itself.
Pro tip: Check weekday hours for fewer people and lower entry fees.

Bondi is more than just its beach - it’s a community of creators, wellness seekers, artists, and locals who’ve made this coastal suburb one of Sydney’s most vibrant places to explore. Step off the main track, slow down, and you’ll uncover hidden gems that many visitors never find.

Bookmark these top spots to elevate your Bondi coffee crawl.
1. BRU
An institution and true Bondi Beach must experience. Sit outside on milk crates around any table that has space alongside locals from all walks of life. This is non-touristy and serves great coffee.
2. Chapter One Coffee & Wine Room

Chapter One Coffee & Wine Room is Bondi Beach’s beloved double-threat café and wine bar perched at the southern end of the beach. Since 2012, it has served gourmet Aussie breakfasts alongside a coffee program that remains one of Bondi’s best. Expertly brewed espressos, velvety flat whites and aromatic filter coffees complement organic acai bowls, eggy brekkies and fresh salads. With beachfront views and open-air seating, Chapter One offers a refined yet laid-back coffee experience.
3. Bennett Street Dairy

Bennett Street Dairy is Bondi Road’s artisanal bakery-café known for in-house baked treats and coffee on tap. House-brewed espresso and creamy flat whites are poured directly from the tap, delivering consistent crema and bold flavour. Pair your caffeine fix with their famous choc-chip cookies or seasonal avocado smash on sourdough. A bright, minimalist interior and crisp white oak finishes make this cafe a go-to for coffee lovers seeking quality beans and sweet indulgences.
4. Speedos Cafe

Speedos Cafe is Bondi’s most Instagrammable café across the road from the beach, pairing panoramic ocean vistas with robust coffee selections. Baristas pull single-origin espressos and craft velvety flat whites that perfectly balance acidity and creaminess. Fuel your morning with a bold long black or a creamy latte, then indulge in their signature pancake towers or giant salad bowls. Bright natural light, surf-inspired décor and beachside seating make Speedos a coffee hotspot.
5. Porch and Parlour

North Bondi’s Porch and Parlour is a beloved beachside café that’s been dishing up breakfast and lunch for over a decade. Expert baristas serve smooth flat whites, robust long blacks and seasonal filter brews alongside cult dishes like pea pancakes and avocado feta toast on house-made ceramics. Pooch-friendly outdoor seating and bright interiors create a relaxed vibe, while ethically sourced beans and precise technique ensure every coffee shines. Porch and Parlour is a coastal must-visit.
6. Harry’s Bondi

Harry’s Bondi sits on Wairoa Avenue, evolving from a hole-in-the-wall espresso bar into a design-forward café known for vibrant flavours and quality coffee. Baristas craft rich espressos, silky cappuccinos and creamy flat whites using ethically sourced beans. Its signature H canned smoothie and matcha drinks push creative boundaries, but the classic long black remains a crowd favourite. With terrazzo counters, palm fronds and ample natural light, Harry’s offers a laid-back yet stylish coffee sanctuary.
7. Lox Stock & Barrel

Lox Stock & Barrel brings New York–style deli vibes to Glenayr Avenue, but its coffee program is equally noteworthy. Baristas pull excellent single-origin espressos, yielding rich crema and bold notes that cut through hearty bagels. Flat whites and cortados showcase creamy milk texture and balanced acidity. Warm wooden interiors and communal tables invite guests to linger over coffee and bagels, making Lox Stock & Barrel a surprising caffeine hotspot in Bondi Beach.
